questions.q: Name the three prime ministers who headed United Front governments between 1996 and 1998, and state which party each belonged to.
questions.a: H.D. Deve Gowda (Janata Dal, June 1996 – April 1997) and I.K. Gujral (Janata Dal, April 1997 – March 1998). A wrong answer (e.g., naming V.P. Singh or Atal Bihari Vajpayee) reveals confusion between the National Front (1989), United Front (1996), and NDA (1998) coalitions, indicating the student has not memorized the distinct coalition phases and their leadership.

questions.q: Why did the Congress party support the United Front government from outside despite being the single largest party in the 1996 Lok Sabha?
questions.a: Congress (140 seats) lacked a majority and refused to join a government led by the Janata Dal (which had split from Congress in 1969), but supported the United Front to keep the BJP (161 seats) out of power. A wrong answer suggesting Congress joined the cabinet or that it supported the BJP shows misunderstanding of the "outside support" mechanism and the anti-BJP polarization that drove 1996 alignments.

questions.q: In 1999, the NDA government lost a confidence motion by a single vote (269–270) after the AIADMK withdrew support. Identify the constitutional provision that governs such a vote and explain the immediate consequence for the Council of Ministers.
questions.a: Article 75(3) of the Constitution states the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a lost confidence motion obliges the Prime Minister to resign. The President then invites the leader of the largest party/coalition to form a government or dissolves the House. A student who cites Article 74 (aid and advice) or Article 356 (President's Rule) confuses executive responsibility with presidential powers, a common error in distinguishing parliamentary accountability mechanisms.

questions.q: Compare the ideological coherence of the NDA (1998–2004) and UPA (2004–2014) coalitions. Which coalition faced greater internal contradiction on economic policy, and why?
questions.a: The NDA combined the BJP's cultural nationalism with regional parties (e.g., TDP, BJD, JD(U)) that prioritized state autonomy and development; its CMP shelved Hindutva issues. The UPA united the Congress's centrist economics with Left parties (CPI(M), CPI) opposing liberalization; this contradiction forced the UPA to dilute labour reforms and stall disinvestment. A wrong answer claiming both were equally coherent ignores the Left's ideological opposition to the UPA's core economic agenda, missing how coalition compulsion shapes policy outcomes.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "Coalition governments between 1996 and 2014 strengthened Indian federalism but weakened the capacity for bold structural reforms." Support your judgment with two specific examples.
questions.a: Valid judgment with examples: (1) Federalism strengthened — regional parties gained cabinet berths (e.g., DMK in UPA, TDP in NDA) and influenced state-specific allocations; (2) Reform capacity weakened — UPA's Common Minimum Programme excluded privatization of PSUs due to Left pressure, and NDA delayed labour law reforms due to coalition objections. A wrong answer that calls coalitions "always unstable" or "always reformist" fails to weigh evidence, showing inability to evaluate trade-offs in democratic governance.

questions.q: Draft a three-point Common Minimum Programme for a hypothetical 2026 coalition comprising a national party committed to fiscal conservatism, a regional party demanding greater state fiscal autonomy, and a left-leaning party opposed to privatization of public sector enterprises.
questions.a: A credible CMP would: (1) Adhere to a glide-path for fiscal deficit (e.g., 3% of GDP by 2028) while allowing states flexibility in borrowing under Article 293; (2) Create a "Strategic Disinvestment" category limited to non-strategic PSUs, with proceeds earmarked for social infrastructure, satisfying fiscal conservatives and partially addressing left concerns; (3) Establish a permanent Inter-State Council secretariat to negotiate GST compensation and central scheme flexibility, empowering the regional party. A poor answer that ignores one partner's core demand (e.g., full privatization) reveals failure to grasp coalition bargaining as interest accommodation.
